content: The ETHE1 protein, also referred to as ethylmalonic encephalopathy 1 protein or persulfide dioxygenase, is encoded by the ETHE1 gene, which is located on chromosome 19 in humans. The ETHE1 gene is composed of seven exons and produces a protein with an approximate molecular weight of 27 kDa. This protein is expressed in the thyroid gland and is predominantly localized to the mitochondrial matrix. Its primary function is as a sulfur dioxygenase, an enzyme involved in sulfur metabolism. Specifically, the ETHE1 protein catalyzes a reaction that requires iron and potentially glutathione as cofactors. The physiological substrate for ETHE1 is believed to be glutathione persulfide, an intermediate metabolite that plays a role in the degradation of hydrogen sulfide. Mutations in the ETHE1 gene are associated with ethylmalonic encephalopathy, a rare metabolic disorder. Patients with mutations in this gene exhibit reduced ETHE1 activity and decreased affinity for its substrate. Mouse models with genetic ablation of the Ethe1 gene also demonstrate impaired sulfide dioxygenase activity and display cranial abnormalities characteristic of ethylmalonic encephalopathy. A reduction in sulfide dioxygenase activity leads to defective hydrogen sulfide catabolism. This results in the accumulation of hydrogen sulfide, a gas-phase signaling molecule in the central nervous system. Excess hydrogen sulfide is thought to inhibit the activity of cytochrome c oxidase, a critical enzyme in the mitochondrial respiratory chain. However, other metabolic pathways may also contribute to modulating the toxic effects of hydrogen sulfide. The ETHE1 protein has been shown to interact with RELA, a component of the NF-κB signaling pathway.
